Number theory. The study of properties and relationships among integers, particularly prime numbers, divisibility, and congruences. Often called the queen of mathematics for its deep elegance and seemingly effortless generation of unsolved problems, number theory bridges abstract algebra and concrete numerical phenomena. Though it originated in curiosity-driven play with integers, modern number theory underlies cryptography, RSA encryption, computer science, and some of mathematics' greatest conjectures.

Divisibility and factors form the foundation. One integer divides another if the result is a whole number. The greatest common divisor and least common multiple capture this structure. Prime numbers are integers greater than one with no divisors except one and themselves. Infinitely many primes exist, as Euclid proved. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic states that every integer greater than one factors uniquely, up to order, into primes. These are the atomic building blocks. Congruences and modular arithmetic capture another essential idea: two integers are congruent modulo n if their difference is divisible by n, written a is congruent to b, modulo n.

Classical theorems shaped the field. Fermat's Little Theorem says that if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a to the p minus one is congruent to one, modulo p. This is crucial for primality testing. Wilson's Theorem states that p minus one factorial is congruent to negative one, modulo p, if and only if p is prime. Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions says infinitely many primes exist in any arithmetic progression a plus k times n where the greatest common divisor of a and n is one. The Prime Number Theorem says the number of primes less than x is approximately x divided by the natural logarithm of x, formalising how primes thin out.

Special integer classes deserve attention. Perfect numbers equal the sum of their proper divisors. Six, for example, equals one plus two plus three. Mersenne primes are primes of the form two to the p minus one. Among the largest known primes, they are tested computationally. Twin primes are pairs of primes differing by two, such as eleven and thirteen. The twin prime conjecture asserts infinitely many exist but remains unproven. Goldbach's conjecture says every even integer greater than two is the sum of two primes. This famous unsolved problem has been tested to astronomical numbers.

Number theory emerged from Greek mathematics, enriched by Islamic scholars and Renaissance mathematicians. For centuries it seemed useless, pure abstraction with no application. The twentieth century proved otherwise. Modular arithmetic and prime factorization underlie RSA encryption, securing Internet commerce. The field has produced some of mathematics' greatest unsolved conjectures like the Riemann hypothesis, Goldbach's conjecture, and the twin prime conjecture, which remain tantalising frontiers.
